accuracy.evidence: Wording follows the National Curriculum in England spoken language statutory requirements for years 1 to 6: gain, maintain and monitor the interest of the listener(s); consider and evaluate different viewpoints, attending to and building on the contributions of others; select and use appropriate registers. The speaking moves (hook, steady pace, clear volume, eye contact, reading audience cues, agree/disagree/add on with a reason, sentence stems) match the Oracy Framework (Voice 21 / University of Cambridge) physical, linguistic, cognitive and social-emotional strands. The only parameterised arithmetic ({=n/2} minutes) uses even n only.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the common slips at 7-8: just naming the topic as an opening, believing fast talk is exciting, reading notes with eyes down, ignoring puzzled or bored faces or a raised hand, a bare 'I disagree' with no reason, a reason that does not fit the stance, attacking the person instead of the idea ('Priya is being silly'), 'just because' as a reason, and using chatty register for a class or school talk.

lab_distinct.evidence: Mechanics are this topic's own: a live class of faces with an attention bar that reacts to the chosen hook, draggable pace and volume dials plus an eyes-up toggle that change each listener's face, four listener signs each needing the right fix, a reply builder that joins a stance stem to a fitting reason and rejects mismatches, and a formal versus informal register sort. It differs from flagbuildon (building on discussions at 10-11) and the register lesson's sorter and passed the 30% shingle gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child sees a weak opening lose the class before being told why a hook works, finds that both too fast and too quiet lose listeners and that eye contact matters, practises monitoring by reading four faces and picking a fix, builds all three kinds of reasoned reply to a peer's view, and chooses register by audience: the three curriculum strands in order (gain/maintain/monitor, viewpoints, register).

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Um, this is about hamsters' as an opening, 'Yes, it sounds exciting' for talking really fast, and 'Yes, it says what I think' for a bare 'I disagree'. Each is overturned by the step's own feedback.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Rotating scenarios (volcano talk opening, disagreeing with a friend's idea, yawning class, whole-school assembly) with nine distinct m= messages naming the slip: no hook, a mumbled start, attacking the person, no reason, rushing, hiding in notes, chatty register for a formal audience, and shouting orders.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences, everyday settings (class talk, show-and-tell, Priya's pet idea) and pass the family kid limit; adult text names the curriculum strands and passes the adult limit. Canvas text is one short heading per step with large wrapped option cards.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and the duplicate gate. Kid text covers hook, pace/volume/eyes, reading faces and reasoned replies; adult text covers curriculum placement, the gain/maintain/monitor model, named reply mistakes, register and what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots of all six steps at start and after Show me in light and dark: the five listener faces and attention bar fit, both dials are full width with large thumbs, the three fix buttons are full width, the reply builder's stems and reasons sit in a 2-column grid with wrapped text, and both register bins fit side by side.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, every task completes with Show me, the challenge shows, no console errors. Every canvas action has a button (hook options, Slower/Faster/Quieter/Louder and eyes toggle, fix buttons, stem and reason buttons, register buttons) and the canvas aria-label reports each result.
